articles.headline: Billings County Election.
articles.text:
Last Monday was not by any means an agreeable day out of doors and this coupled with the lack of excitement, caused the number of voters to be but little more than half the number who had been registered. The polls opened promptly at eight o'clock in Paddock's livery office. The greatest rush of voters was during the first hour, when a number of rail-road men who had not been registered had to swear in their votes. There had been just 122 votes cast at five o'clock when the polls closed. The result showed a much larger amount of scratching than was expected, some entirely new names running well. The following is the vote in full:

COMMISSIONERS.
J. W. Goodall. 121
Dan. McKenzie. 122
J. L. Truscott. 122
REG. OF DEEDS & CO. CLERK.
J. C. Williamson. 122
SHERIFF.
Fred. A. Willard. 122
ASSESSOR.
Willis L. Eaton. 112
George Fitzgerald 9
PROBATE JUDGE.
T. W. Gordon. 56
E. L. Simmers. 63
John Warn 1
TREASURER.
W. F. VanDriesche. 122
COUNTY SURVEYOR.
D. O. Sweet. 49
Arthur W. Smith. 72
CORONER.
Talleyrand Martin. 122
SUP'T. OF PUB. SCHOOLS.
Wm. Dantz. 122
JUSTICES.
Gregor Lang, 48
Norman Lebo, 120
J. C. Copeland, 114
E. Elmer. 121
J. A. Copeland, 8
G. Gorham Bond, 70
CONSTABLES.
J. B. Harmon, 119
Fred. Banan, 57
John Creedon, 87
J. W. Tompkins. 122
M. Coleman, 67
H. R. Tarbell, 1
J. R. Grymes, 35
COUNTY SEAT—MEDORA. 121

"STICKERS"

122 votes polled.

The judges and clerks had the hardest work of any. Their siege of fourteen hours, with no intermission, was harder than sawing wood.

Mr. McGinness made a good supervisor. In case any of his decisions had not given satisfaction, a glance at his frame would have discouraged the average objector.

There were three different kinds of tickets used. There being a chance for four or more stickers on the regular ticket, the result in some cases, was unexpected.

J. R. Grymes made a good run for constable. He didn't stay with the leather long enough, though.

When one of the judges makes a man who is swearing in his vote show up his teeth to decide his age and then remarks that his statements are "tooth in," it calls for gore.

The fact that no one could vote whose name was not registered, until he had sworn his vote in, caused several to believe that their vote was challenged.

Gill Kennnedy deserves and has the everlasting thanks of the officers of election for a large pail of delicious lemonade.

John Warn was again remembered by one of his Medora friends. "Alaska John" would have "got there, dead or alive" if he had been present.

The way Mike Coleman's name bobbed up for constable, knocked calculations "galley west for election."

Some good hits on Democrats would not have been mede in the poll room, if all had known that Supervisor Mc Ginness was one of the strongest Democrats in Dakota.

The danger of one person depending on others to do what he should do himself, was well illustrated in the election of surveyor. Arthur Smith refused to run under any circumstances. He is not a citizen and would not have accepted the office if he had been. Consequently he resigned in favor of D. O. Sweet, who consented to run more as a matter of accommodation than anything else, as it is doubtful if there is anything in the office except the empty honor. As it was so well understood that Arthur would not serve if he could, everyone expected that Sweet would get the highest number of votes and consequently neglected to substitute his name for Smith's, whose name appeared on the ticket as the nominee of the convention.
articles.summary: Full returns and sidelights from Monday's Billings County election at Paddock's livery office: 122 votes cast, Medora chosen county seat, and Arthur Smith elected surveyor despite refusing to serve.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a book entitled "A Texas Cowboy," written by C. L. Siringo, and printed by Siringo & Gibson, Chicago. It has not, nor does it pretend to have any claims of a literary value, but it is written in cowboy language and is descriptive of many phases of cowboy life. The author's description of the manner in which herds were started in early days, with a pony and a branding-iron is especially interesting. Looked at from the cowboy point of view, it is a truthful account of the hardships a cowboy voluntarily or involuntarily endures.

articles.headline: Meeting of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association.
articles.text:
The fourth semi-annual meeting of the above association was called to order by Chairman Theodore Roosevelt, at the town hall, last Monday morning at half past ten.

The roll being called by Secretary J. L. Truscott, nearly all members answered to their names.

The minutes of the last meeting were read and approved.

W. A. Merrifield proposed the name of L. C. Hunt for membership. The chairman stated that unless there was objection he would decide that as membership in the Association was by firms and as E. W. Casey & Co. already held membership, there was no necessity of electing Mr. Hunt, he being representative of E. W. Casey & Co. There being no objection, it was so held and Mr. Hunt's name was enrolled as a member.

The report of the secretary was read, showing the association to be free from debt and a cash balance in the treasury.

Willis Eaton moved that John Goodall be elected foreman of the spring round-up. There being no further nominations the motion was unanimously carried.

On motion of Willis Eaton, it was decided to start the round-up on or about June 1. at the mouth of Box Elder. Working down the Little Missouri to the mouth of Beaver, thence up Beaver to its head.

On motion of J. L. Truscott, it was decided that the committee appointed to go to Miles City, be instructed to recommend the above at that meeting.

It was moved by J. L. Truscott and carried that J. N. Simpson and Theodore Roosevelt be appointed the committee to represent this association at the Miles City meeting. These two members also to have power to choose a third. Also that the committee be instructed to recommend that J. N. Simpson and Henry Boice be the members of the executive committee from Dakota.

As moved by Willis Eaton and amended by J. L. Truscott a motion was made and carried, that mavericks be given to the owner of the range on which they are found. In case of dispute, the matter is to be left to arbitration, each party in dispute choosing a representative and these to choose one, two or three more.

On motion of D. K. Wade, this resolution was ordered embodied in the by laws of the association.

W. A. Merrifield brought up the subject of branding cattle between Dec. 1 and the spring round-up.

On motion of Willis Eaton, a resolution was carried to the effect that members shall not be allowed to work cattle between Dec. 1 and the spring round-up and that in other respects our rules should conform to those of the Montana association on the subject.

J. L. Truscott moved that the association stand by Jos. McCoul and others in their action in reference to an animal in dispute between them and the Bad Lands Cattle Co. On calling the roll, there were found to be eight yeas and seven nays. The chair stated that on account of the peculiarity of the vote and that as it was a subject to demand greater unanimity and without in any manner expressing an opinion on the merits of the case he should vote nay and declare the motion lost.

Association adjourned.

"ROUND-UPS."

Messrs. Ferris and Burdette represented the 13 outfit.

Mr. Arnett of Arnett & Thomas, represented the ΛHΛ brand at the meeting.

There was a larger attendance than at any previous meeting of the association.

Messrs. Towers, [Boice?], [Wibaux?], Grisy, Rowe, Tarbell and Morrison were present from Mingusville.

A. N. Jeffries will, after the general round-up, start an outfit to work the country on the river below our round-up district.

Messrs. Marney of the Stockgrowers' Journal, Knight of the Yellowstone Journal, Mabee of the Glendive Times and Widmyer of the Independent, were present.
articles.summary: Proceedings of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association's fourth semi-annual meeting, chaired by Theodore Roosevelt: Goodall chosen round-up foreman, June 1 start set, Roosevelt and Simpson named delegates to Miles City, and a maverick rule adopted.

articles.headline: Perfect Gun Sights.
articles.text: In the BAD LANDS COW BOY this week will be observed the advertisement of Lyman's gun sights, which are probably about as near perfect as will be reached in this century. His rear sights are universally used by hunters and riflemen throughout Europe and America, and, when used with his new ivory bead front sight which is here illustrated, an ordinary marksman can bore the bulls-eye with astonishing accuracy, and kill running game with ease. The American Field recently published engravings of targets made with these sights, showing that out of seventeen shots, all struck within the bulls-eye but one, which struck the line between bulls-eye and center. We have received a sample of the sight, and will take pleasure in showing it.
articles.summary: Editorial notice of Lyman's gun sights, a sample of which is at the Cow Boy office.

articles.headline: Alfalfa in Dakota.
articles.text:
If he who makes two blades of grass grow where only one grew before, is a public benefactor, then whatever will cause the soil to grow more fodder and extend the season of growth six or eight weeks is also a benefactor.

Alfalfa will do this. It is a clover nearly related to red clover. It is as hardy, if not hardier. Rooting deep it is quite independent of the rain fall. It starts earlier in the spring than the grasses and continues to grow after they are dead.

Mr. J. R. Lowe, of Bijou Hills, Dak., writes me that five years ago he received from the Agricultural Department a package of alfalfa, which he scattered thinly over a patch of ground that had been worked two years and paid no more attention to it. Naturally the weeds took possession but the alfalfa caught. For three years the weeds had the upper hand and being an eyesore he mowed them. But the following year being very dry the alfalfa gained ascendency, and in the spring of '85 every plant was in its place alive and vigorous and showed its color three weeks before anything else started, and was full six inches high before cattle could live on the prairie. He is absolutely certain that not a plant has died from any cause, that it extends the time of green feed at least two months in the year, early frost not killing it down; that it is worthy of trial, and he has great hopes that it will prove a success in Dakota.

There is ample proof that it will stand our cold winters. At Highmore, Dak., there are five acres, sown last spring, that made a good growth. It was visited by a hail storm, but being a tough stalk was not cut as badly as the wheat. Specimens I have from the field, in fact show no effects of the hail.

It was a standing temptation to the pigs of the neighborhood, and whenever they got out they took a near way to the alfalfa. At Blunt, Mr. Zollers pulled from his patch a plant whose root measured twenty-two and a half inches, the growth of one season. At Miller, Hand Co., an eighth of an acre sowed on sod last spring made a splendid growth. I observed reeds on the stalks which were left standing to help it through the first winter. It was alive and in good condition the 8th. of February when examined. At this place, an experimental patch, by its growth enthused us with a belief in its future.

I hear some one ask what if it does yield eight or ten bushels to the acre yearly after it is well set, what is it good for?

It is relished by all kinds of stock; it takes the place of corn; alfalfa fed beef resembles corn fed; pigs riot in it, and grow fat during the mild months by having portable fences on different lots, as it will not stand constant feeding; it will enable Dakota to compete with the corn states in raising stock; it will produce an abundant yield every year in spite of hail, frost or drought; it will renew the soil. Dakota cannot always grow small grain. It is only a question of time when the present culture will exhaust the soil. I look to alfalfa as the stepping stone to profitable stock raising, a sure foundation to any country's prosperity.—[Northwestern Farmer.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Northwestern Farmer urging alfalfa as fodder for Dakota stock raising.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a telegram from Tilden R. Selmes, stating that he has procured an injunction on the treasurer of Stark county preventing him from collecting taxes of Billings Co. By this time the injunction has been served on the treasurer by the sheriff. This will make a stay of proceedings until the constitutionality of the law can be properly decided.
articles.summary: Tilden R. Selmes telegraphs that he has procured an injunction against Stark County taxing Billings County.

articles.text: We received last evening a copy of the injunction, issued through Attorney Selmes by Judge Francis. It restrains the treasurer of Stark county from ever collecting taxes from Billings county, provided the charges made are proved. It might be well to state that there are several new charges made and if they are proved it will render the assessment null and void, whether the law authorizing it is constitutional or not. Mr. Selmes will be in Medora in a few days.
articles.summary: Copy of Judge Francis' injunction received; Selmes expected in Medora.

articles.text: Theodore Roosevelt returned Monday from a successful chase after the men who stole his boat about three weeks ago. Sewell and Dow accompanied him on the trip and they overtook the thieves about a hundred miles down the river. Mr. Bad Man Finnegan tried some of his old tactics and refused to return but such sound arguments were advanced that he concluded to change his mind. The prisoners were brought across the country to Dickinson and from there were sent to Mandan for trial. They will be sent up for as long a time as the law allows.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt, with Sewall and Dow, captured the boat thieves including Finnegan about a hundred miles downriver and delivered them via Dickinson to Mandan for trial.

articles.text: There are still several tax-payers who have not signed the agreement to pay their pro rata in contesting the legality of the law under which we are taxed by Stark Co. The paper was left with us by Howard Eaton for additional signatures and we hope to see every tax-payer represented on it. This contest is something in which every tax-payer is interested and the only fair thing is for each tax-payer to pay his share of the expenses. The pro rata to be fixed by the amount assessed against each tax-payer. This will make the share of each insignificant. This being a matter of such public concern, no one should depend on his neighbors' paying his share.
articles.summary: Appeal for taxpayers to sign Howard Eaton's agreement to share costs of the Stark County tax contest.

events.title: Billings County holds election; Medora chosen county seat
events.summary: Billings County voters cast 122 ballots at Paddock's livery office, electing Goodall, McKenzie and Truscott commissioners, Willard sheriff, and naming Medora the county seat by 121 votes. Turnout was about half the registration on a disagreeable day.
events.excerpt: There had been just 122 votes cast at five o'clock when the polls closed.

events.title: Arthur Smith elected Billings County surveyor despite refusing to run
events.summary: Arthur W. Smith, not a citizen, had withdrawn in favor of D. O. Sweet, but voters neglected to substitute Sweet's name and Smith out-polled him 72 to 49.
events.excerpt: Arthur Smith refused to run under any circumstances. He is not a citizen and would not have accepted the office if he had been.

events.date_basis: "April 19" stated; future relative to Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: Montana Stockgrowers' Association spring meeting at Miles City
events.summary: The Montana Stockgrowers' Association's spring meeting was to open at Miles City on April 19.
events.excerpt: The spring meeting of the Montana Stockgrowers' association begins at Miles City, April 19.

events.title: Lloyd Roberts to deliver Counell herd at Dickinson
events.summary: Lloyd Roberts was expected in Medora about the 25th, delivering Aleck Counell's herd at Dickinson for Counell's Cave Hills ranch.
events.excerpt: Lloyd Roberts will arrive in Medora about the 25th., delivering at Dickinson Aleck Counell's herd for his Cave Hills ranch.

events.title: Joint outfit to work the Grand River country
events.summary: The N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. and Bad Lands Cattle Co. planned to start an outfit about the 17th to work the Grand River country, likely with an outfit from the E6.
events.excerpt: will start an outfit about the 17th. to work the Grand river country, probably from its source to its mouth.

events.title: Wm. Dantz unloads 300 Minnesota heifers at Medora
events.summary: Wm. Dantz arrived with 300 two-year-old heifers from Minnesota and unloaded them at the stock yards; he was to leave next morning to receive 350 more bought in Iowa.
events.excerpt: Wm. Dantz arrived this morning with 300 two-year-old heifers and unloaded at the stock yards.

events.date_basis: Undated receipt notice; week before Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: Cow Boy reviews Siringo's "A Texas Cowboy"
events.summary: The Cow Boy acknowledged receipt of C. L. Siringo's "A Texas Cowboy," calling it a truthful account of cowboy hardships though without literary pretension.
events.excerpt: it is written in cowboy language and is descriptive of many phases of cowboy life.

events.title: Theodore Roosevelt chairs Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association meeting
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt called the association's fourth semi-annual meeting to order at the Medora town hall; attendance was the largest yet.
events.excerpt: was called to order by Chairman Theodore Roosevelt, at the town hall, last Monday morning at half past ten.

events.title: Roosevelt and Simpson named delegates to Miles City stockmen's meeting
events.summary: On J. L. Truscott's motion, J. N. Simpson and Theodore Roosevelt were appointed to represent the association at the Miles City meeting, with power to choose a third member, and to recommend Simpson and Henry Boice for the executive committee from Dakota.
events.excerpt: J. N. Simpson and Theodore Roosevelt be appointed the committee to represent this association at the Miles City meeting.

events.title: John Goodall elected foreman of the spring round-up
events.summary: On Willis Eaton's motion, John Goodall was unanimously elected foreman of the spring round-up.
events.excerpt: Willis Eaton moved that John Goodall be elected foreman of the spring round-up.

events.date_basis: "on or about June 1" decided at meeting of Mon 12 Apr 1886
events.title: Spring round-up to start at mouth of Box Elder
events.summary: The association decided to begin the round-up on or about June 1 at the mouth of Box Elder, working down the Little Missouri to the Beaver and up Beaver to its head.
events.excerpt: it was decided to start the round-up on or about June 1. at the mouth of Box Elder.

events.title: Association adopts maverick and winter-branding rules
events.summary: Members voted that mavericks go to the owner of the range where found, with disputes arbitrated, and that no cattle be worked between Dec. 1 and the spring round-up.
events.excerpt: mavericks be given to the owner of the range on which they are found.

events.title: Roosevelt casts deciding vote in McCoul–Bad Lands Cattle Co. dispute
events.summary: A motion to back Jos. McCoul and others in a dispute over an animal with the Bad Lands Cattle Co. carried eight to seven, but chairman Roosevelt, citing the need for greater unanimity, voted nay and declared it lost.
events.excerpt: he should vote nay and declare the motion lost.

events.title: Ranchers and Montana editors attend stock meeting
events.summary: Ranchers from Mingusville and editors Marney (Stockgrowers' Journal), Knight (Yellowstone Journal), Mabee (Glendive Times) and Widmyer (Independent) attended; Ferris and Burdette represented the 13 outfit.
events.excerpt: Messrs. Marney of the Stockgrowers' Journal, Knight of the Yellowstone Journal, Mabee of the Glendive Times and Widmyer of the Independent, were present.

events.date_basis: Planned "after the general round-up"; reported Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: A. N. Jeffries to work river below the round-up district
events.summary: A. N. Jeffries planned to start an outfit after the general round-up to work the river country below the association's district.
events.excerpt: A. N. Jeffries will, after the general round-up, start an outfit to work the country on the river below our round-up district.

events.title: H. T. Hallcck of Mandan visits Medora
events.summary: H. T. Hallcck of Mandan was in town.
events.excerpt: H. T. Hallcck of Mandan, was in town Monday.

events.date_basis: Present tense "is in town"; week before Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: Wells-Fargo route agent in Medora
events.summary: E. A. Stedman, the Wells-Fargo route agent, was in town.
events.excerpt: E. A. Stedman, the Wells-Fargo route agent is in town.

events.title: H. B. Wadsworth arrives, goes to home ranch
events.summary: H. B. Wadsworth arrived Monday night and went out to the home ranch.
events.excerpt: H. B. Wadsworth arrived Monday night and has gone to the home ranch.

events.title: Marquis de Morès and wife return from hunt down the river
events.summary: The Marquis and his wife returned from their hunt down the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: The Marquis and wife returned from their hunt down the river, last evening.

events.date_basis: Stock meeting held "last Monday" before Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: J. P. Small and son attend stock meeting
events.summary: J. P. Small and son, from north of the Yellowstone, attended the stock meeting.
events.excerpt: J. P. Small and son, from north of the Yellowstone, attended the stock meeting.

events.title: Little Missouri low enough to cross
events.summary: The river was so low it offered no impediment to crossing, though the quicksands were as treacherous as ever.
events.excerpt: The river is now so low that it offers no impediment to crossing.

events.title: Rain gives grass a fresh start
events.summary: A Tuesday night rain gave the grass a fresh start, and in many places green had replaced the old grass.
events.excerpt: The refreshing rain of Tuesday night gave the grass a fresh start

events.date_basis: Miles City meeting opens April 19; reported Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: Half-rate rail fares for stockmen to Miles City meeting
events.summary: Stockmen and their families could travel to the Miles City meeting at half rate: full fare going and a pass returning.
events.excerpt: Full fare must be paid going and a pass will be given returning.

events.title: Freight conductor M. Linsley run over at Dickinson
events.summary: Freight conductor M. Linsley was run over at Dickinson; his leg was amputated and he was recovering in the hospital at Brainerd.
events.excerpt: Freight conductor M. Linsley, who was run over last week in Dickinson is now in the hospital at Brainerd.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday evening" before Thu 15 Apr 1886; left Wednesday
events.title: Bismarck Tribune editor M. H. Jewell visits Medora
events.summary: Editor M. H. Jewell of the Bismarck Tribune came down Tuesday evening and returned Wednesday morning; on his last visit Medora had been only sage-brush and a dug-out.
events.excerpt: The last time he was here, Medora consisted of sage-brush and a dug-out.

events.title: Refrigerator Car Co. serves tax injunction on Stark County treasurer
events.summary: The N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. obtained an injunction restraining the Stark County treasurer from collecting Billings County taxes; George Cole had the papers served.
events.excerpt: George Cole, as representative of the Co. had the papers served yesterday.

events.date_basis: Stock meeting "last Monday" before Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: Roosevelt praised for running the stock meeting
events.summary: Many complimented Mr. Roosevelt's handling of the stock meeting, where useless or irrelevant discussion was brought to a sudden stop.
events.excerpt: There were numerous complimentary remarks at Mr. Roosevelt's method of conducting the stock meeting.

events.title: J. A. Ferris named Collins agent in Medora
events.summary: C. R. Kelsey of J. S. Collins & Co. appointed J. A. Ferris sole agent for Collins goods in Medora, with a full stock at Ferris' store.
events.excerpt: has appointed J. A. Ferris the sole agent for the Collins' goods in Medora.

events.date_basis: Telegram received before Thu 15 Apr 1886; injunction served by then
events.title: Selmes wins injunction against Stark County taxing Billings County
events.summary: Attorney Tilden R. Selmes telegraphed that he had procured an injunction stopping the Stark County treasurer from collecting Billings County taxes until the law's constitutionality is decided.
events.excerpt: he has procured an injunction on the treasurer of Stark county preventing him from collecting taxes of Billings Co.

events.title: Cow Boy receives copy of Judge Francis' tax injunction
events.summary: The Cow Boy received a copy of the injunction issued by Judge Francis through Attorney Selmes, restraining Stark County from collecting Billings County taxes if the charges are proved.
events.excerpt: It restrains the treasurer of Stark county from ever collecting taxes from Billings county, provided the charges made are proved.

events.date_basis: "in a few days" after Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: Attorney Selmes expected in Medora
events.summary: Tilden R. Selmes was expected in Medora in a few days.
events.excerpt: Mr. Selmes will be in Medora in a few days.

events.title: Roosevelt returns after capturing boat thieves
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt returned from pursuing the men who stole his boat; with Sewell (Sewall) and Dow he overtook them about a hundred miles down the river, and Finnegan was persuaded to surrender. The prisoners were taken overland to Dickinson and sent to Mandan for trial.
events.excerpt: Theodore Roosevelt returned Monday from a successful chase after the men who stole his boat about three weeks ago.

events.date_basis: "about three weeks ago" before Thu 15 Apr 1886
events.title: Roosevelt's boat stolen
events.summary: Men stole Theodore Roosevelt's boat about three weeks before the issue.
events.excerpt: the men who stole his boat about three weeks ago.

events.title: Taxpayers urged to sign agreement funding Stark County tax contest
events.summary: An agreement left by Howard Eaton at the Cow Boy office sought signatures from Billings County taxpayers to share pro rata the cost of contesting Stark County's taxation.
events.excerpt: The paper was left with us by Howard Eaton for additional signatures
